articles.title: From Bytes to Glyphs: How Computers Actually Understand and Display Text
articles.excerpt: I was solving the Anagram exercise in Go when a single word stopped me: rune. I had written a loop to count characters, and Go handed me a rune instead of a byte or a char. I knew it had something to…
articles.body: I was solving the Anagram exercise in Go when a single word stopped me: rune . I had written a loop to count characters, and Go handed me a rune instead of a byte or a char . I knew it had something to do with Unicode, but I couldn't have told you what a rune really was, or why len() sometimes disagrees with the number of characters I can see. One small type led to a lot of questions. What is Unicode, and does it assign bits to characters? How does UTF-8 fit in? And why do some screenshots show text as a row of empty boxes? This post follows how I worked through those questions. Every Go snippet below compiles and runs, and the outputs are real.

articles.title: Gating an Agent Reverse-Engineering Runner Behind Next.js Server Actions
articles.excerpt: We did not adopt morluto/rea to reverse engineer other people's software. We needed a repeatable pass over artifacts we already ship: the client bundle from our Next.js 15 app, and a small native help…
articles.body: We did not adopt morluto/rea to reverse engineer other people's software. We needed a repeatable pass over artifacts we already ship: the client bundle from our Next.js 15 app, and a small native helper that rides with the desktop build. The project describes agents that walk app behavior down toward native binaries, which matched the two layers we actually own. Hanging that runner off the same app that produces the artifacts failed in two places that had nothing to do with disassembly quality. The first failure was a secret in the client bundle. A shared module imported server-only config so the runner could read a model key. A form later gained "use client" and pulled a value import from that module instead of import type . The compiler followed the edge.

articles.title: Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe
articles.excerpt: The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.
articles.body: The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun. The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar. The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.

articles.title: November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)
articles.excerpt: From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.
articles.body: The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names , often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze. November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons , which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

articles.title: SpaceX launches secretive spy satellites from California for US Space Force (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched its fifth classified mission for U.S. national security this month today (Nov. 24), from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
articles.body: SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT) , carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month. While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .

articles.title: 'Blade Runner 2099' executive producers talk architectural easter eggs and franchise continuity for Prime Video's new sci-fi series (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''
articles.body: Prime Video's new " Blade Runner 2099 " series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising. This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, " Blade Runner ." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.
